content: Trichomes, derived from the Greek word meaning growth of hair, are fine outgrowths or appendages found on plants and certain protists. These structures exhibit a wide range of forms and functions, including hairs, glandular hairs, scales, and papillae. Algal Trichomes In certain filamentous algae, the terminal cell extends into an elongated, hair-like structure known as a trichome. This term is also used to describe similar structures in some cyanobacteria. Plant Trichomes Aerial Surface Hairs Trichomes on plants are epidermal outgrowths of various types. Outgrowths that involve more than just the epidermis are referred to as emergences or prickles, though this distinction is not always straightforward. For example, some non-trichomatous epidermal cells may protrude from the surface. A common type of trichome is the hair, which can be unicellular or multicellular, branched or unbranched. Multicellular hairs may consist of one or several layers of cells. Another common type of trichome is the scale or peltate hair, which is a plateor shield-shaped cluster of cells attached directly to the surface or borne on a stalk. Any type of hair may also be glandular. When describing the surface appearance of plant organs such as stems and leaves, various terms are used to denote the presence, form, and appearance of trichomes. The most basic terms are glabrous (lacking hairs) and pubescent (having hairs). More specific terms include: Glabrous, glabrate: Lacking hairs or trichomes; surface is smooth. Hirsute: Coarsely hairy. Hispid: Having bristly hairs. Downy: Covered with an almost wool-like layer of long hairs. Pilose: Pubescent with long, straight, soft, spreading, or erect hairs. Puberulent: Minutely pubescent; having fine, short, usually curly hairs. Pubescent: Bearing hairs or trichomes of any type. Strigillose: Minutely strigose. Strigose: Having straight hairs all pointing in more or less the same direction, such as along a margin or midrib. Villosulous: Minutely villous. Villous: Having long, soft hairs, often curved but not matted. Hairs on plants vary greatly in their presence across species, their location on plant organs, their density (even within a single species), and their functionality. However, several basic functions or advantages of surface hairs can be identified. For instance, plant hairs may deter feeding by small herbivores and, depending on their stiffness and irritability, may also discourage larger herbivores. In frost-prone areas, hairs help protect living surface cells from frost damage. In windy environments, hairs disrupt airflow across the plant surface, reducing evaporation. Dense coatings of hairs can reflect solar radiation, shielding delicate tissues beneath in hot, dry, open habitats. In regions where moisture primarily comes from cloud drip, hairs may enhance the collection of this moisture. Root Hairs Root hairs, which are rhizoids found in many vascular plants, are tubular outgrowths of trichoblasts, the hair-forming cells on the epidermis of a plant root. These structures are lateral extensions of a single cell and are rarely branched. Before root hair development, there is a localized increase in phosphorylase activity. Root hairs typically measure between 5 and 17 micrometers in diameter and 80 to 1,500 micrometers in length (as noted by Dittmar, cited in Esau, 1965). They have a lifespan of 2 to 3 weeks before dying off, while new root hairs are continuously formed at the root tip. This ensures consistent root hair coverage. It is important to handle plants with care during repotting, as root hairs are often stripped away in the process. This is why plants may appear wilted for some time after being transplanted.
